transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-04 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Park (Redwood SE), Alicia Morales (CTO, Kryptonix), Raj Patel (Lead ML Eng), Dana Lee (Security Arch), Omar Ruiz (SRE)

Summary (auto): define POC success metrics, gather traffic signature, decide on hosted vs dedicated for pilot, and agree benchmark steps and timeline.

00:00:03 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining on a monday arvo — i think the plan is we run through what success looks like for the pilot and the workload signal, ok?
00:00:10 Alicia Morales: yeah thanks maya, appreciate it, quick context — Kryptonix is rolling out a contextual assistant inside our dev console, expecting peak hours when teams push large searches, so we care about tail latency and cost.
00:00:24 Raj Patel: clarifying, our typical interactive path is a prompt -> 1-2 shot context -> generated code snippet, so input tokens average around 110, output around 70 but we have tail cases up to 1,600 tokens for long code dumps.
00:00:40 Jonah Park: ok good, that's useful. when you say tail, is that like 1% of traffic or more?
00:00:45 Raj Patel: ballpark 3–4% past 512 tokens, and maybe 0.5% past 1024.
00:00:52 Maya Chen: great, so early notes: token mix skewed-right, a small heavy tail. for sizing we'll want mean input ~110, mean output ~70, with 95th and 99th quantiles captured.

00:01:15 Dana Lee: quick security note — for pilot we need a private control plane or peered VPC, all logs must be encrypted with our KMS, and retention capped at 30 days unless we sign a special data agreement. is that possible?
00:01:29 Maya Chen: absolutely. we support a private deployment (Redwood Private) or dedicated capacity with VPC peering; we also have KMS integrations, we can map the key policies. jonah will run through specifics.
00:01:40 Jonah Park: yeah, on the KMS side we do customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and you can set retention TTLs in the console. small caveat: some audit traces are longer-lived for debugging but we can gate that with RBAC.

00:02:05 Omar Ruiz: for the benchmark we can expose a test subnet, but we want to ensure the replay traffic won't leak secrets — we'll sanitize payloads first.
00:02:12 Maya Chen: perfect. next — success criteria. what's the go/no-go for you?
00:02:20 Alicia Morales: must-haves: 95th percentile latency under 300ms for our main interactive path at 50 sustained QPS during peak; scalability to 200 QPS burst with graceful degradation; correctness — generation quality equivalent to our current model baseline (we'll provide eval prompts); and security controls as dana mentioned.
00:02:45 Maya Chen: that is super actionable — to restate: 95p < 300ms at 50 qps, survive bursts to 200 qps, quality parity on eval set, and VPC+KMS. are there cost thresholds that would kill the deal?
00:02:58 Alicia Morales: yes — our CFO set a soft cap of $0.02 per 1k tokens for pilot phase, otherwise we'll have to push back.
00:03:08 Maya Chen: good to know — we'll model cost. jonah, can we run cost estimates for that token mix?
00:03:13 Jonah Park: yes, we'll run cost per token with batching and cache assumptions. two important knobs: batching window and prefix caching — both affect latency/cost tradeoff. for example continuous batching to 16 tokens increases throughput, but adds 20–40 ms under low QPS.

00:03:40 Raj Patel: can we see the effect numerically? like 50 qps with mean 180 total tokens per request?
00:03:47 Jonah Park: quick offhand: with our recommended config (batching=16, kv cache warm for 60% of requests), you might see per-token cost drop ~30% and 95p latency comfortably under 300ms at 50 QPS on a 4-GPU dedicated pool. but we need to run your trace to confirm.

00:04:10 Maya Chen: ok benchmark plan: customer provides an anonymized 48h production trace, include timestamps, prompt length, response lengths, and a flag for quality-critical paths. Redwood will provide a replay harness (kafka/httpreplay), an infra manifest for a dedicated 4-GPU bench and a hosted baseline. we'll run both and share latency/cost and tail quantiles.

00:04:37 Alicia Morales: what about concurrency? our frontend creates spikes — often dozens concurrent requests per user when they paste code blocks. so concurrency shape matters.
00:04:47 Jonah Park: yes concurrency profile is critical. please include inter-request spacing and concurrency per session in the trace. we'll run a shape-based replay: steady-state 50 QPS, with injected bursts to 200 QPS for 10 minute windows. we'll measure p50/p95/p99 and p999 if possible.

00:05:10 Raj Patel: we can annotate the trace with which requests we consider high-precise (goldens) vs casual. those should be routed to higher-cost model variants?
00:05:18 Maya Chen: that's a common pattern — routing by priority. for the POC we can test two variants: single-model baseline and a mixed routing policy (cheaper model for casual, high-quality model for goldens) to show cost savings.

00:05:33 Dana Lee: another security question: audit logs — can you provide immutable audit trails for model calls? we need to show who invoked what and when.
00:05:40 Jonah Park: yes, we ship per-request audit logs with request id, model id, route, and token counts. retention and redaction policies are configurable.

00:05:55 Omar Ruiz: network setup — how fast is peering? we want <3 ms added latency between our app and model endpoints.
00:06:02 Maya Chen: with VPC peering in the same region we typically see <2–4 ms network overhead. if we need sub-ms we'd look at colocated on-prem options.

00:06:18 Alicia Morales: timeline expectation? 4 weeks? what are the milestones?
00:06:22 Maya Chen: we propose a 4-week pilot: week 0 (this week) — kickoff + trace handoff; week 1 — infra + replay harness config and baseline hosted run; week 2 — dedicated pool runs and tuning (batching, kv cache), week 3 — evaluation, quality tests and security signoff, end of week 4 — go/no-go and pricing discussion.

00:06:42 Raj Patel: is the dedicated pool pre-provisioned? we cannot wait long for GPUs.
00:06:47 Maya Chen: for pilots we offer fast provisioning; typical spin-up is 24–48 hours for reserved dev pools. if there's a strict window we can pre-reserve for the benchmark run.

00:06:59 Jonah Park: one more note on the workload signature: include token histograms (input/output), sequence length quantiles, and the request inter-arrival distribution — poisson vs bursty — because kernel selection in the runtime adapts to sequence length mixes and that changes perf.

00:07:20 Raj Patel: we'll export histograms — one ask: can you run quantile latency by token length bucket? like 0–128, 128–512, 512–1024, >1024?
00:07:28 Jonah Park: yes, that's part of the standard benchmark report. we also provide concurrency heatmaps and per-model throughput numbers.

00:07:36 Alicia Morales: about quality evaluation — we'll share an eval set of ~250 prompts with gold answers. we expect pass rate similar to our current infra. how do you measure generation parity?
00:07:47 Maya Chen: we run automated n-gram and embedding-based similarity plus a small human review set. we'll produce a quality delta table and flag any regression >3% as a blocker.

00:07:59 Dana Lee: do you do model fingerprinting to ensure the model variant matches the version in the catalog? we need reproducibility for audits.
00:08:06 Jonah Park: yes we include model hashes and deterministic seeds for evals where possible, and we version artifacts. small note: some non-determinism is expected with sampling but eval harness accounts for it.

00:08:20 Raj Patel: initial sizing question: if our steady-state is 50 qps and mean 180 tokens total, what's the expected GPU footprint for the dedicated pool?
00:08:29 Jonah Park: rough estimate: for your token mix and tail, a 4x A100-equivalent pool with our runtime and batching should handle 50 steady qps with comfortable headroom; for the burst to 200 qps we'd rely on autoscale and graceful shedding or routing to cheaper variants. exact numbers after replay.

00:08:50 Maya Chen: let's capture acceptance criteria again so there's no ambiguity. i'll read back: 95th percentile latency <300ms at sustained 50 QPS for main path; handle 200 QPS bursts for short windows with graceful degradation; quality parity on customer eval set (delta <3%); VPC peering + KMS + audit logs; cost target ~$0.02 per 1k tokens for pilot. any misses?
00:09:12 Alicia Morales: that's correct.
00:09:15 Dana Lee: add data retention 30 days unless otherwise agreed.
00:09:18 Maya Chen: noted.

00:09:28 Maya Chen: objections — typical thing we see is cost vs latency; you may need to accept small latency increase to meet the $0.02/1k token. any preference?
00:09:38 Alicia Morales: we prefer latency first for dev UX but willing to trade a bit for cost if it's minor — ideally please show a graph of the tradeoff.
00:09:47 Jonah Park: we will. we'll produce a cost-latency curve with points for batching and routing policies.

00:09:55 Raj Patel: another practical detail — do you support request routing by request metadata? we want to route by project_id and priority header.
00:10:02 Jonah Park: yes, headers and routing rules are supported; we can set per-route qps and rollout policies.

00:10:12 Omar Ruiz: on observability — will you expose token-level billing and per-route latency? we need that for chargeback internally.
00:10:19 Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdown and per-route dashboards. we'll give you access to a demo tenant for visibility.

00:10:28 Alicia Morales: about regulatory — any region constraints? we need EU data residency for some accounts; will that affect our pilot?
00:10:35 Maya Chen: pilot in a US region is fine for initial tests; for production we can provision EU region endpoints. for the POC we just need to ensure data is stored in your region if required.

00:10:48 Raj Patel: ok to confirm deliverables from Redwood: harness, baseline hosted run, dedicated run, perf report with quantiles by token bucket, cost modeling, and sample routing policy.
00:10:58 Maya Chen: yes that's what we'll deliver.

00:11:05 Jonah Park: small transcribe glitch — we sometimes conflated K V cache as k v catche in earlier notes — but to be clear it's KV cache, key-value cache for context.

00:11:15 Dana Lee: timeline for security review — we can do a short checklist and then a deeper SOC2 mapping if pilot looks good.
00:11:23 Maya Chen: we'll have our security brief ready; i'll send it along with the harness.

00:11:30 Alicia Morales: thoughts on how to validate quality in a reproducible way? human review plus automated metrics?
00:11:35 Jonah Park: exactly, automated similarity metrics + 30 human evals on a stratified sample. will flag hallucinations and functional regressions.

00:11:44 Raj Patel: anything about the model itself? are you bringing an open checkpoint or a proprietary model? we need licensing clarity.
00:11:51 Maya Chen: we can host open models and provide Redwood-verified model profiles. if you choose a Redwood-managed licensed model we'll include terms. we'll document model ids and versions in the report.

00:12:05 Alicia Morales: ok i think we have enough to start. quick question — what's the expected time to get preliminary numbers after you get the trace?
00:12:12 Jonah Park: baseline hosted run within 48 hours of trace ingestion, dedicated run within 72 hours from infra spin-up, so ~5 business days to preliminary numbers.

00:12:24 Maya Chen: perfect. to close, recap next steps: maya sends harness and pricing; raj provides trace and eval; jonah prepares benchmark configs; dana and mayas security teams sync.
00:12:36 Alicia Morales: yep. thanks everyone.
00:12:39 Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark run. bye.
